lessons.title: Metals and the reactivity series
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Chemistry — Properties of metals, reactivity series, corrosion, extraction of iron and aluminium, alloys (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: State physical and chemical properties of metals.
Order metals in the reactivity series from their reactions with water, acid and oxygen.
Explain how reactivity relates to corrosion and extraction.
reviewNotes: Order used: potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, (carbon), zinc, iron, (hydrogen), copper, silver, gold. Lead and tin sit between iron and hydrogen in most tables.
Aluminium appears unreactive because of a protective oxide layer.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Properties of metals
blocks.md: Metals are typically **shiny, malleable, ductile, hard and dense**, good **conductors** of heat and electricity, with high melting points (exceptions: sodium, mercury). They form **positive ions** and their oxides are **basic**. **Alloys** are mixtures of metals (or metal + carbon) that are often harder or more resistant to corrosion than the pure metal.

blocks.title: The reactivity series
blocks.md: **K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, (C), Zn, Fe, (H), Cu, Ag, Au** (most to least reactive). K, Na and Ca react with **cold water** (H₂ + hydroxide); Mg reacts slowly with cold water and quickly with **steam** (oxide + H₂); Zn and Fe react with steam; metals above **hydrogen** react with dilute acids giving H₂; Cu, Ag, Au do not react with dilute acid or water. Reactivity is also the order of ease of **forming positive ions** and of **corrosion**.

blocks.title: Displacement
blocks.md: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu (blue colour fades, brown copper forms). A reaction occurs **only** if the added metal is **more** reactive than the metal in the solution. Metal oxides can be displaced similarly: magnesium reacts with copper(II) oxide on heating.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.md:
- Carbon and hydrogen are placed in the series for comparison but are not metals.
- Aluminium is high in the series but protected by a thin layer of aluminium oxide, so it seems unreactive.
- Never put potassium or sodium in water without teacher supervision.

blocks.caption: The reactivity series (simplified): potassium at the top, silver at the bottom.
blocks.alt: A vertical arrow with the symbols K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Cu and Ag from most reactive at the top to least reactive at the bottom.

blocks.title: Example 1 — will it react?
blocks.statement: Will iron displace copper from copper(II) sulphate solution? Will copper displace zinc from zinc sulphate solution? Give the equation where a reaction occurs.
steps: Iron is above copper in the series, so it displaces it: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu (brown copper forms on the iron).
Copper is below zinc, so no reaction occurs with zinc sulphate.
blocks.answer: Yes for iron; no for copper

blocks.title: Example 2 — placing unknown metals
blocks.statement: Metal P reacts slowly with cold water; Q does not react with water but gives bubbles with dilute acid; R does not react with water or acid. Place P, Q, R in order of reactivity.
steps: P reacts with cold water, so it is the most reactive. Q reacts with acid but not cold water: less reactive than P.
R does not react with acid: the least reactive. Order: P > Q > R.

lessons.title: Extraction of iron and aluminium
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level Chemistry — Properties of metals, reactivity series, corrosion, extraction of iron and aluminium, alloys (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Explain how the method of extraction depends on the position in the reactivity series.
Describe the blast furnace extraction of iron with equations.
Describe the extraction of aluminium by electrolysis.
Calculate masses of metals from ores; state uses of steel and other alloys.
reviewNotes: Cameroon has an aluminium smelter at Edéa (ALUCAM) and bauxite deposits; the smelter and its raw material sources should be checked before being named in class.
Temperature ~950 °C for molten alumina in cryolite and the 1500–2000 °C zone of the blast furnace are typical textbook values.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Choosing the method
blocks.md: Most metals occur as **ores** (compounds, mainly oxides). Reactive metals (above carbon: K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al) are extracted by **electrolysis** of molten compounds; metals below carbon (Zn, Fe, Pb, Cu) can be extracted by **reduction with carbon or carbon monoxide** (heating the oxide with coke). Unreactive metals (gold, silver) occur as native metals.

blocks.title: Iron: the blast furnace
blocks.md: Raw materials: **iron ore** (haematite, Fe₂O₃), **coke** (carbon), **limestone** (CaCO₃), hot **air**. Reactions: C + O₂ → CO₂ (heat); CO₂ + C → 2CO; **Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂** (reduction). Limestone: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂; CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃ (**slag**, removes sand). Molten iron and slag run off at the bottom (slag is less dense and floats). Iron is made into **steel** by removing carbon and impurities with oxygen.

blocks.title: Aluminium: electrolysis
blocks.md: Bauxite is purified to **aluminium oxide (alumina), Al₂O₃**. Alumina has a very high melting point, so it is dissolved in molten **cryolite** (about 950 °C) to save energy. **Cathode** (carbon lining): Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al (molten metal collects at the bottom). **Anode** (carbon): 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻; the oxygen burns the carbon anodes to CO₂, so they must be replaced. The process needs **large amounts of electricity**, so smelters are located near cheap hydroelectric power.

blocks.title: Alloys and uses
blocks.md: **Steel** (iron + carbon): stronger than iron (buildings, tools); **stainless steel** (iron + chromium + nickel): does not rust. **Brass** (copper + zinc), **bronze** (copper + tin). Aluminium (low density, resists corrosion): cooking pots, aircraft, overhead cables. Copper: electrical wiring. Zinc: galvanising.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.md:
- Iron(III) oxide is reduced by carbon monoxide, not by the limestone; limestone only removes the sand as slag.
- Aluminium is not extracted in the blast furnace: it is above carbon in the reactivity series.
- The carbon anodes burn away during aluminium electrolysis and must be replaced regularly.

blocks.caption: A blast furnace: raw materials go in at the top, hot air at the bottom; slag and molten iron are tapped from the base.
blocks.alt: A tall furnace shape with arrows for the raw materials entering at the top, hot air entering near the bottom and slag and molten iron leaving.

blocks.title: Example 1 — iron from haematite
blocks.statement: Calculate the mass of iron obtainable from 160 g of iron(III) oxide: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ (Fe 56, O 16).
steps: Ratio Fe₂O₃ : Fe = 1 : 2, so n(Fe) = 2 mol; mass = 2 × 56 = 112 g.

blocks.title: Example 2 — aluminium from alumina
blocks.statement: Calculate the mass of aluminium obtainable from 102 kg of aluminium oxide: 2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂ (Al 27, O 16).
steps: Mr(Al₂O₃) = 2 × 27 + 3 × 16 = 102, so 102 kg is 1000 mol. Ratio Al₂O₃ : Al = 1 : 2, so n(Al) = 2000 mol.
